item.text: {"text":"NextItNet uses stacked dilated causal convolutions and residual connections to capture longer histories; its architectural receptive field establishes which positions can influence predictions, not which positions the trained model actually uses. Count every convolution’s dilation when calculating coverage. [Original NextItNet paper](https://fajieyuan.github.io/papers/nextitnet6.pdf). Recent work explicitly measures sequential-recommendation recency bias and reports that excessive recent-item emphasis can hurt accuracy; recency dependence alone therefore does not establish useful temporal reasoning. [Measuring Recency Bias, 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722).\n\nActivation-patching research supports comparing clean and selectively modified inputs, caching activations, and restoring chosen components to measure output recovery. Results depend strongly on corruption design, patch location and evaluation metric. [Interpretation guidance, 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.15255); [metrics and methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16042). Proposed adaptation: separately replace older-prefix versus recent-suffix items while preserving sequence length, left-padding and untouched positions; temporarily patch residual-block outputs and, where present, the prefix-mean gate’s inputs/output. Keep the final-nonpadding readout and candidate set fixed. Report paired candidate-rank changes alongside score margins, with identity patches and matched unrelated-donor patches as sham controls. Test both restoration and disruption directions within the same trained category model. These experiments characterize model dependence under specified interventions; they do not establish causal user intent. The sources found provide methodological support, rather than a validated NextItNet-specific patching protocol from 2024–2026."}
